reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Sialadenitis is inflammation of a salivary gland, most commonly affecting the parotid or submandibular gland
Acute bacterial infection typically develops in dehydrated, debilitated or postoperative patients with reduced salivary flow, classically ascending parotitis
It presents with a painful, tender, swollen gland, and gentle massage may express pus from the duct opening in the mouth
Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism in acute suppurative parotitis, whereas viral parotitis (mumps) is a key non-bacterial cause
Submandibular sialadenitis is often related to a stone (sialolith) obstructing the duct, causing pain and swelling that worsen at mealtimes
General measures such as good hydration, oral hygiene, warm compresses, gland massage and sialogogues promote salivary flow and recovery, alongside appropriate antibiotics for bacterial disease
An enlarging, fluctuant, non-resolving gland may indicate abscess formation needing drainage
Recurrent or chronic sialadenitis warrants imaging to look for stones, strictures or an underlying mass or systemic disease
reference.pathophysiology: Salivary glands are normally protected from ascending infection by continuous salivary flow, which flushes the ducts, and by antibacterial constituents of saliva. When flow is reduced, by dehydration, poor oral intake, debility, medications that dry the mouth, or mechanical obstruction from a duct stone or stricture, oral bacteria ascend the duct and infect the gland, producing acute suppurative sialadenitis with parenchymal inflammation and pus. Stasis of saliva also predisposes to stone formation, and calculi in turn obstruct outflow, causing painful mealtime swelling and recurrent infection. Repeated episodes lead to chronic inflammation, ductal changes and glandular fibrosis. Viral sialadenitis such as mumps causes a non-suppurative inflammatory swelling.
additionalDifferentials: Salivary duct calculus without active infection
Sjogren syndrome and other autoimmune sialadenitis
Sarcoidosis or IgG4-related disease of the salivary glands
Reactive cervical lymphadenopathy near the gland
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound of the gland to assess for stones, abscess or a mass
Culture of pus expressed from the duct or obtained at drainage
Plain radiography or CT to detect calculi
Sialography or MR sialography for ductal anatomy in recurrent disease
Blood tests including inflammatory markers and, where relevant, mumps serology and autoimmune screening
Fine needle aspiration or biopsy if a neoplasm is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly spreading swelling, systemic sepsis or airway compromise from a deep neck or floor of mouth extension (an emergency)
A persistent hard gland mass, facial nerve weakness or skin fixation suggesting malignancy
Fluctuant swelling indicating an abscess requiring drainage
Failure to resolve with appropriate treatment, prompting imaging and reassessment
Bilateral gland involvement with systemic features suggesting a systemic or autoimmune cause
reference.prognosis: Acute bacterial sialadenitis usually resolves with rehydration, salivary stimulation and antibiotics, and outcomes are good when the cause is treated; recurrent obstruction from stones or strictures and chronic sialadenitis may require repeated treatment or gland surgery.
pitfalls: Overlooking dehydration and reduced salivary flow as the precipitant, especially postoperatively
Missing an obstructing calculus in recurrent mealtime swelling
Assuming all salivary swellings are infective and overlooking a tumour
Delaying drainage of an established abscess
Neglecting facial nerve assessment when a hard parotid mass is present
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Empirical antistaphylococcal antibiotics such as flucloxacillin for acute suppurative bacterial parotitis, later tailored to culture of expressed pus
Rehydration and correction of the reduced salivary flow that predisposes to ascending infection
Stimulation of salivary flow with sialogogues, gland massage, warm compresses and good oral hygiene
Analgesia and anti-inflammatory measures for the painful, tender gland
Ultrasound to identify an abscess or obstructing stone, with needle or surgical drainage of any collection
Supportive care alone for viral parotitis such as mumps, which does not require antibiotics
Treatment of underlying ductal obstruction from stone or stricture and ENT referral for recurrent disease
